name: PT WEHA Transportasi Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: WEHA Transportasi Indonesia: a cash-generative coach and shuttle operator priced for a high hurdle
frontmatter.summary: WEHA runs Indonesia's best-known tourism coach fleet and the DayTrans intercity shuttle on a capital structure the market treats as impaired. Restated depreciation lifts EBITDA to 27.0% of revenue, nine-month revenue grew 11.3%, and the shares trade at half book with a covered dividend. BUY, on a target set at the most likely path rather than the most bullish one.
thesis: The data pack understates total depreciation roughly threefold; on the LK's own charge EBITDA is IDR85.9bn, and the shares are on 2.3x forward EBITDA.
Intercity shuttle (DayTrans) revenue grew 15.4% in the first nine months of 2026 while legacy coach charter grew 5.3%; the mix shift is the growth engine.
At 19.4% of revenue the business grows about as fast as its returns justify, and the cash it throws off after that capex is what the market is not paying for.

The discount is a governance and liquidity discount, not an operating one: at half book the equity is worth more than the price on every valuation method we run, and the bear case — four points less growth, a margin squeeze and a rate shock — is worth about half the price, which is the risk a holder takes.
Risks are real and named: high-speed rail on the Jakarta-Bandung corridor, fuel and toll inflation, a controller with two-thirds of the shares, related-party capital allocation, and a small float.

catalysts.event: Year-end holiday season: the peak quarter for both the coach charter and the shuttle
FY2026 audited results: confirmation that the second half held the intercity growth rate
Dividend for FY2026 declared; a fourth consecutive year at the same DPS would confirm the policy
Electric minivan trial outcome on the Jakarta-Semarang corridor

blocks.text: **BUY**, target Rp155, expected return 75.9% against a price of Rp92. This is an initiation and the call is deliberately uncomfortable: the shares are illiquid, the controller owns most of the company, and the discount we are underwriting has persisted for years. But the operating evidence does not support the price, and the price itself tells us what the market is assuming.

The variant view is about the depreciation line. The data pack carries a D&A charge of a fraction of what the audited accounts show: the LK's total D&A for FY2025 is IDR51.6bn, of which IDR3.4bn is right-of-use depreciation and the rest is the fixed-asset charge in the property note [S2], against a pack figure roughly a third of that. Because the pack rebuilds EBITDA off that line, every screen built on it understates the EBITDA margin by a wide margin. The accounts show EBITDA of IDR85.9bn on revenue of IDR317.7bn, a margin of 27.0% [S2]. That is the difference between a bus company that looks like it barely covers its fleet cost and one that generates IDR73.5bn of operating cash flow.

What the market is pricing. At Rp92 the equity is worth 0.5x forward book and 5.3x forward earnings, with a dividend yield of 7.3% [S0]. Our reverse DCF says the current price requires about five points off every forecast year's revenue growth — the FY2027E rate of 8.5% falls to 3.6%, and the path decelerates from there to low single digits while terminal growth stays at 4.0% — from a company whose revenue grew 11.3% in the first nine months of 2026 [S6]. Read the other way, the price is what our own cash flows are worth at a discount rate about four points above our WACC, which is the required-return story the float explains.

Three things move the value: whether intercity shuttle growth of the last year is a route-expansion cycle that persists or a one-off; whether the returns the fleet earns justify the capital it absorbs while capex stays near a fifth of revenue; and whether the associate stake and the related-party relationship are worth book value or a discount to it. We assume the first persists at a fading rate, the second is true at roughly today's incremental return, and the third at book with the governance risk carried in the discount rate and the liquidity haircut.

Indonesian land transport is a low-multiple industry by nature: buses are depreciating assets, the
customer buys a seat, and nobody pays a scarcity premium for a fleet. The value in these businesses
comes from utilisation and from financing structure rather than from pricing power. That is why a coach
operator with a well-known brand can trade at a discount to book for years without anything being wrong
with the operations, and why the market price alone is weak evidence about the business.

WEHA Transportasi Indonesia runs three land-transport businesses from a Jakarta head office, under brands better known than the listed ticker [S2]. The company was founded as Panorama Transportasi and renamed in 2015 [S2]; it is controlled by the Tirtawisata family through the Panorama travel group. The annual report's shareholder table shows 52.5% held by PT Panorama Sentrawisata, 14.5% by PT WEHA Investama and 33.0% held by the public below the five per cent disclosure threshold [S2]. The index-style free float the data pack carries is a fifth of the shares once holdings it does not treat as free float are excluded [S0]; we use the smaller figure for the liquidity haircut and the AR figure for control.

**Coach charter (White Horse Deluxe Coach).** The original business: tourist and corporate coach rental across Java, Sumatra and Bali, in three vehicle classes (big coach, medium coach and minivan), including premium sub-brands for luxury and business-class configurations [S2]. Revenue was IDR124.0bn in FY2025, about two-fifths of the group [S2]. This is the segment the market thinks of when it thinks of WEHA, and it is the one that struggled: utilisation fell from seventy per cent in 2024 to 64.0% in FY2025 as household purchasing power weakened, and revenue fell four per cent [S2]. Management's answer is to push corporate employee shuttles and school runs, which are contracted rather than episodic [S2]. In the first nine months of 2026 the segment grew 5.3%, so it has stopped shrinking but has not recovered [S6].

**Intercity shuttle (DayTrans).** Scheduled executive minivan services on the Jakarta-Bandung corridor and across Central and East Java, sold through counters in the cities it serves and through an online booking system [S2]. Revenue was IDR185.0bn in FY2025, up thirteen per cent, and it is now the larger of the two operating segments [S2]. In the first nine months of 2026 the segment grew 15.4% while coach charter grew 5.3% [S6]. This is the growth engine and the competitive battleground.
**Travel and other.** Domestic open-trip and private tour packages sold through the Explorer.id app, plus small car rental [S2]. It is a rounding item at about three per cent of revenue [S2].

**Assets and people.** The group operated 431 buses vehicles at the end of 2025, up from a fleet just above four hundred a year earlier, with 650 drivers trained drivers, five coach offices and forty-four shuttle counters [S2]. The fleet is the balance sheet: property and equipment net, plus right-of-use assets and advances on fleet ordered but not delivered, of IDR294.8bn is most of the asset base [S2].

**Group and control.** WEHA is a subsidiary of PT Panorama Sentrawisata Tbk, the listed travel group [S0, S2]. Control sits with the Tirtawisata family; the president director and the finance director are both family appointments [S0]. A 35.9% stake in PT Andalan Selaras Abadi, a related party that holds land used as collateral for the company's bank facilities, is carried as an associate at IDR41.5bn [S2]. What that stake earns is negligible, a loss of a few million rupiah a year [S2], but it is a tenth of the asset base and we value it.

WEHA sells capacity in three adjacent markets: tourism coach charter, scheduled intercity shuttle, and packaged domestic travel. All three are domestic-demand businesses tied to household spending, holiday calendars and the state of the toll-road network, and all three are fragmented: coach charter in particular has many regional operators and no participant with pricing power [S2].

The demand drivers that matter are the ones our macro deck carries: real growth and inflation set the envelope for discretionary travel, and the rupiah matters twice over because it prices the imported chassis and spare parts the fleet runs on and it sets the cost of the fuel the fleet burns [deck.macro]. Management names exactly these as the cost pressures it fought in 2025: toll increases on several sections, restrictions on subsidised fuel in some areas, and higher spare-part prices [S2].

**The competitive threat that matters is rail.** The Whoosh high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung is being scheduled for up to sixty-two services a day over the year-end Nataru 2026/2027 holiday period — the peak timetable, not the normal one — with the operator targeting sixteen to twenty-three thousand passengers a day against normal-day volumes ten to fifteen per cent lower [S7]. DayTrans' core corridor is Jakarta-Bandung. The rail service does not destroy the shuttle market — the shuttle runs from more city-centre points and at lower fares — but it caps the premium end of it, and it is the single best explanation for why the market will not pay a growth multiple for the fastest-growing segment [S7, S2].

**Competitive position.** WEHA's advantages are real but modest. Distribution density is the strongest: forty-four shuttle counters plus the online channel give DayTrans a reach a new entrant would have to buy [S2]. Brand recognition in coach charter is genuine after five decades [S2]. Switching costs are low for charter customers and near zero for a shuttle passenger who can book a competitor on a phone, and there are no network effects. On the five-forces view: supplier power is high because chassis and parts are imported and priced off the dollar; buyer power is high for corporate charter and moderate for retail shuttle; the threat of new entrants is high in charter and moderate in shuttle because counter reach is expensive to replicate; and the threat of substitutes — rail, low-cost airlines, and the private car on the new toll roads — is the binding constraint. Rivalry is intense and price-led, which is exactly what the FY2025 margin compression records [S2].

**Regulation.** Tourism transport requires an operating licence from the Directorate General of Land Transport, and WEHA's current licence runs to December 2027 [S2]. That is a renewal event rather than a near-term risk, but it sits on the catalyst list because a licence is the one asset the company cannot buy back quickly. Fuel subsidy policy is the second regulatory lever: restrictions on subsidised diesel are a direct cost event and management has already flagged them [S2].

Overland transport in Java has been structurally advantaged by the toll-road build-out of the past
decade, which cut journey times between the big cities and made scheduled road shuttle services
competitive with short-haul flights on the same routes. The same build-out, however, made it easier for
new operators to enter, which is why route density and counter networks, not vehicle quality, have
become the defensible assets in intercity shuttle.

**The depreciation restatement.** The single most important adjustment in this model is D&A. The data pack carries a charge that is a fraction of the audited figure because IDX filings use the direct cash-flow method and the depreciation add-back is not visible where a data vendor looks for it. The audited note is explicit: total depreciation and amortisation of IDR51.6bn was charged in FY2025, of which IDR3.4bn is right-of-use depreciation and the remainder is the property-note fixed-asset allocation split between cost of revenues and general and administrative expenses [S2]; FY2024 was IDR44.8bn [S2]. Restating both years rebuilds EBITDA: the engine now carries IDR85.9bn for FY2025 on revenue of IDR317.7bn, a 27.0% margin. This is not a cosmetic reclassification; it changes the EBITDA multiple by a factor of about two and a half.

**Revenue and margin history.** Revenue rose from IDR183.4bn in FY2022 to IDR317.7bn in FY2025, a compound path built first on the post-pandemic recovery of tourism charter and then on intercity shuttle expansion [S2]. The mix moved against the gross margin: coach charter earns more per vehicle-day than a scheduled minivan seat, so as shuttle grew to more than half of revenue the group gross margin fell to 35.4% from the levels of the recovery years [S2]. Operating expenses did not fall with it, because SG&A is largely drivers, workshop and counter staff, so operating margin compressed to 10.8% and net margin to 7.0% [S2].

**FY2026 to date.** First-half revenue was IDR168.7bn with the gross margin at 36.0% [S5]. Nine-month revenue reached IDR256.0bn, and net profit attributable to owners was IDR17.8bn, flat to slightly below the same period of 2025 [S6]. The company's own target for 2026 is revenue and net profit up 10.0% [S2]. Revenue is running ahead of that; profit is not. Our FY2026E net profit of IDR25.3bn is above both the last actual of IDR22.2bn and the plan, and it is therefore the most aggressive line in the model, because it needs a fourth quarter well above the fourth quarter of 2025 — the peak holiday quarter that produced the weakest result of that year. Two anchors carry it, both of them the last audited actual rather than a better number from a half-year filing: SG&A at 24.6% of revenue, the FY2025 rate, where the first half of 2026 printed a little higher; and other non-operating income at the FY2025 recurring level, where first-half disposal gains were running at roughly a third of the prior year's [S2, S5]. Neither is evidenced as recurring, and if the second half holds the half-year run-rate instead, FY2026E net profit lands nearer the company's own plan than our figure. The higher interest charge and the smaller gain on asset sales are what offset the operating improvement [S5, S6].

**Cash flow, capex and the fleet.** Operating cash flow was IDR73.5bn in FY2025 [S2], comfortably above net profit, which is what a capital-intensive business should look like. Capex was IDR61.7bn, of which the cash purchase of property and equipment was the largest part, with right-of-use additions, intangibles and advances for fleet ordered but not delivered making up the rest [S2]. Capex has run at roughly a fifth of revenue for two years while the fleet grew to 431 buses units [S2]. The investment case turns on what that ratio buys: at 19.4% of revenue the business spends about three points of revenue more than it depreciates, which funds the fleet's growth, and the return on that incremental capital is roughly ten per cent — adequate, not exceptional. Capex does not fade to replacement in our base case, because a company growing four per cent nominal at a seven-and-a-half per cent return has to keep investing; what changes is that the depreciation charge is measured properly, so the cash left after capex is visible rather than hidden behind a data-vendor artefact [S2].

Our forecast has revenue growing 11.3% in FY2026, the nine-month actual, fading to 5.5% by FY2030; gross margin held at 35.5%, which is where the first half actually printed; SG&A at 24.6% of revenue, the FY2025 audited run-rate; capex at 19.4% of revenue throughout; and other non-operating income carried at the FY2025 actual level of recurring disposal gains rather than at zero [S2, S5].

**Forecast against the plan, and what the first draft got wrong.** FY2026E revenue of IDR353.6bn and net profit of IDR25.3bn sit above the company's own +10.0% target, because revenue is running at the nine-month rate rather than the plan rate and because we restore the disposal gain the first draft zeroed [S2, S6]. The four earlier departures are gone: the audited SG&A ratio of the last actual replaces the rounded figure of the first draft; other non-operating income is carried at the FY2025 level of a recurring kind rather than at zero; the DPS no longer falls below the flat nominal dividend paid three years running; and FY2026E is no longer modelled below the last actual [S2, S5]. The P/E leg lifts with the higher earnings and the dividend roll-forward with the higher DPS; together the four restorations were worth a low-double-digit number of rupiah per share.

**Owner earnings.** The bridge from reported profit to owner earnings is short, and it is why we trust the EBITDA restatement: net profit of IDR22.2bn plus the total depreciation charge of IDR51.6bn reconciles to the operating cash flow of IDR73.5bn [S2]; after capex of IDR61.7bn and a working-capital release in the year, free cash flow to the firm was IDR25.4bn, about eight per cent of revenue. Nothing in that bridge is an accounting artefact: the cash is either in the operating line or sunk in the fleet. The forecast year holds the same shape — capex of IDR68.6bn against D&A of IDR57.3bn, for free cash flow to the firm of IDR15.8bn — so growth is funded from operations and the dividend is not being borrowed.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Total interest-bearing debt was IDR116.8bn at end-2025 against cash of IDR32.0bn, for net debt of IDR84.8bn, or 1.0 EBITDA [S2]. The stack is two different things wearing one label. Bank loans were IDR38.7bn — a short-term facility, the current portion of long-term loans and the long-term remainder [S2] — written at seven and a half to eight per cent and secured partly on land owned by the associate [S2]. The rest is fixed-asset purchase payables owed to fleet vendors: the company takes delivery, pays over time, and the payable sits in liabilities [S2]. That distinction matters in the risk section, because vendor payables are a rolling fleet-financing facility, not a bullet the company must refinance in a bad year.

Liquidity is tight in the accounting sense — the current ratio was one at end-2025, down from one and a quarter, as bank loans and fleet payables came due within the year [S2]. It is not tight in the cash sense: operating cash flow covers the current portion several times over [S2].

**Earnings quality.** On our screens WEHA passes. The accruals ratio is strongly negative — net profit of IDR22.2bn against operating cash flow of IDR73.5bn — meaning earnings are backed by cash rather than by working capital [S2]. Receivables run at fourteen days and the shuttle business is largely prepaid [S2]. Inventory is spare parts and small [S2]. There is no capitalised development cost of consequence [S2]. The auditor's opinion is unqualified in every year of the report's five-year history table [S2]. Related-party sales were IDR5.1bn in H1-2026, about three per cent of revenue, priced on the same terms as third-party sales [S5]. The two flags we carry are structural rather than accounting: the associate subscription described in the governance section, and the fact that gains on asset sales recur often enough to be part of the earnings base rather than exceptional [S2].

We value WEHA on discounted free cash flow to the firm, cross-checked against P/E and P/BV. The industry registry assigns sixty per cent to the DCF, twenty-five to EV/EBITDA and fifteen to P/E; we have set the EV/EBITDA weight to zero and given the free weight to P/BV. That is a deliberate rejection, not a convenience: the peer multiples the engine can compute come from the same data packs that understate D&A, so a peer EV/EBITDA median of roughly nine times is measured on a denominator three times too small. Applied to our restated EBITDA it would have valued the equity at roughly four times the DCF and contributed more than the DCF itself to the weighted target. A multiple computed on a wrong denominator cannot be applied to a right one. The house comps sheet for the same land-transport names carries EV/EBITDA of about three times once their own D&A is restated, and at three times this equity is worth roughly the DCF, so nothing is lost by dropping the leg. P/BV is the natural asset cross-check for a business whose balance sheet is a fleet, and its peer multiples are on real book value.

The cost of equity is 15.8%, and it is built exactly as the engine computes it: a risk-free rate of 7.4% less a 1.6% default spread, plus a levered beta of 1.48 applied to a mature equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%. The unlevered beta is 0.90, the industry median regression beta for land transport, geared to 1.48 by a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.83 at market values. Two things about that build matter. First, the gearing is measured on all interest-bearing liabilities, and about half of them are fixed-asset purchase payables owed to fleet vendors — trade finance, not bank debt — so the levered beta overstates financial risk rather than understating it; on bank facilities alone the leverage, and the beta, would be roughly half as large. Second, we do not add a separate small-cap premium on top: the house constitution requires illiquidity to be shown as its own line in the target, never hidden in the discount rate, and it is: the target is struck after a 10.0% haircut for a stock whose average daily traded value over three months is 523,535,430 rupiah against a market capitalisation of 134,371,043,348 rupiah [S0]. The ladder is explicit: a traded value below the half-billion-rupiah mark earns double this haircut, and below a fifth of that it triples. WEHA sits just above the first threshold, so the deduction shown is the mildest rung the house allows, and a further deterioration in traded value would take the target down accordingly; even the harshest rung, a tripling of the haircut shown, would leave the target above today's price, since the probability-weighted value before any haircut is Rp172. The WACC of 11.9% sits inside the house band for rupiah assets.

The DCF produces Rp138 per share on an enterprise value of IDR254.7bn, 49.4% of which sits in the terminal value. The compounder card is why that share is no longer higher. In the first draft the terminal year reinvested only about a fifth of its NOPAT to grow four per cent, which implies an incremental return near twenty per cent on new capital against roughly seven and a half per cent the company earns today — a step-change nothing in the accounts supports. We have therefore held capex at 19.4% of revenue through the terminal year, the rate the company actually spent in FY2025 [S2]: net reinvestment of about three points of revenue, plus working capital, is a little over forty per cent of the NOPAT margin, and four per cent growth on that reinvestment rate implies an incremental return of roughly ten per cent — in line with the capital the company already employs. The explicit-period capex sums to more than the depreciation charge, so the business adds net assets as it grows rather than distributing them.

The multiple-survival test, with both numbers on one basis. Excluding the associate from the numerator and the denominator alike — as the DCF itself does, since it keeps the associate outside enterprise value and adds it after — today's price is a little under twice forward EBITDA, about one and four fifths on the forecast balance-sheet net debt and a little under two on the 30 June figure the DCF actually deducts. The terminal value is about two and a third times terminal-year EBITDA on that same basis. So, stated plainly: the DCF assumes the exit multiple expands, by something of the order of a third to half a turn, and not that it compresses. We cannot source a re-rating, and we do not pretend otherwise. What the terminal value does is capitalise the terminal year's free cash flow at a discount rate of 11.9% with growth of 4.0%; the multiple that produces is what a buyer requiring our WACC would pay for the mature fleet, and the whole of the gap to today's entry multiple is the required-return gap the float explains elsewhere in this section. A reader who refuses to pay more than today's entry multiple for the terminal value gets a DCF per share about a tenth lower — roughly the P/BV cross-check of Rp119, still above the market price — and a weighted value about three-tenths above the price, so the call does not rest on the re-rating. The forward multiple printed in the tables, 2.3x, is not on this basis: it carries the associate inside enterprise value with none of its earnings in the denominator, which is why it looks higher than the entry multiple quoted here and why it is not the number to set against the terminal value.

The cross-checks now bracket the primary method from below rather than contradicting it. P/E values the equity at Rp102 on 6.7 times earnings (-25.8% against the DCF) and P/BV at Rp119 on 0.7 times book (-13.8%). Both use the same six land-transport peers — BIRD, BLTA, SMDR, CASS, ASSA and JAYA — rather than the whole logistics registry, which mixes tanker operators and airport handlers into the median. The gap between them and the DCF is the usual one for an asset-heavy operator: earnings and book capitalise the fleet at its historical return, while the DCF capitalises the cash the fleet will throw off once the depreciation charge is measured properly. We keep the DCF at the primary weight because the cash is what a buyer receives, and we report the weighted value of Rp128 as the fair value, with the base-case twelve-month target at Rp141.

**What the price implies.** Run backwards, today's Rp92 is consistent with a growth path in which every forecast year's revenue growth is cut by about five points — the FY2027E rate of 8.5% becomes 3.6%, the FY2028E rate follows it down to about two and a half, and the fade years come in under one — while terminal growth stays at 4.0%. That is not "no growth for ever", but it is a path that decelerates to low single digits and then runs below the terminal rate it is meant to converge to, which is internally inconsistent and contradicts nine-month revenue growth of 11.3% [S6]. Run the other solve and the price is consistent with a discount rate roughly four to five points above our WACC at normal growth. Of the two, we believe the discount rate. The growth path the reverse DCF implies is not a forecast any operator would make; a required return in the mid-to-high teens is exactly what a market applies to a company with a 33.0% public holding, no analyst coverage, no index membership and a daily traded value that rounds to nothing [S0]. The call is that the operating evidence does not justify that required return — not that the market has mis-forecast the business.

Sensitivity is dominated by the discount rate and by capex. A one-point move in WACC changes the DCF value by roughly a sixth; the capex ratio matters through the same channel, because every point of revenue held in buses is a point of free cash that never reaches the shareholder. Revenue growth matters less than either, which is the useful discipline here: this is a cash-conversion and cost-of-capital story, not a growth story.

**Regulatory and licence (low likelihood, high impact).** The tourism transport licence runs to December 2027 [S2]. Renewal is routine for an operator with a clean record, but the licence is non-substitutable and a suspension would stop the coach business.

**High-speed rail substitution (high likelihood, medium impact).** Whoosh is scheduled for up to sixty-two Jakarta-Bandung services a day over the year-end Nataru 2026/2027 peak, carrying an expected sixteen to twenty-three thousand passengers a day [S7]. The DayTrans corridor is the same city pair. We assume intercity growth decelerates from 8.5% rather than collapsing, but this is the risk that most directly attacks the growth half of the thesis.

**Cost inflation and fuel policy (high likelihood, medium impact).** Toll increases, restrictions on subsidised diesel and imported spare parts priced off the dollar all hit the gross margin directly; management named each of them as a 2025 cost driver, and the margin fell accordingly [S2]. Our base case holds the margin at the H1-2026 level rather than assuming recovery [S5].

**Consumer demand (medium likelihood, high impact).** Coach charter utilisation fell from seventy per cent to 64.0% in one year on weak purchasing power [S2]. A second leg down takes the charter business back to loss-making at the contribution level.

**Leverage and refinancing (low likelihood, medium impact).** Net debt of IDR84.8bn is 1.0 EBITDA and the current ratio is one [S2]. The debt is amortising fleet finance rather than a bullet, which makes it manageable, but a sharp rate rise lifts a charge that already consumes about a third of operating profit [S2].

**Governance and related parties (certain, medium impact).** The controlling group holds almost two-thirds of the shares — 52.5% Panorama Sentrawisata and 14.5% WEHA Investama — against 33.0% public [S2]. The company has shown willingness to move large sums to related entities: it paid IDR40.5bn of cash in 2024 for new shares in an associate, raising its stake from under two per cent to 35.9%, in an entity whose contribution to earnings is a rounding error [S2]. That is a tenth of the asset base and roughly a third of the market capitalisation at today's price. We size the related-party exposure in the next section; the point for the valuation is that we carry the stake at book because the money was paid in cash and the entity holds the land securing the company's own bank facilities, and we carry the governance risk in the discount rate and the liquidity haircut rather than as a second deduction.

**Liquidity (certain, high impact for a fund).** The AR shows 33.0% of the shares in public hands, but the index-style free float is smaller at one-fifth of the shares [S0, S2], and daily traded value is a fraction of the market capitalisation [S0]. A position of any size cannot be built or exited at the screen price. This is the risk that no amount of operating performance fixes, and it is why the target is struck after the liquidity haircut rather than being a twelve-month price prediction.

**The gate result, stated rather than implied.** The engine's investability gate fails this name: a market capitalisation of 134,371,043,348 rupiah and an average daily traded value of 523,535,430 rupiah are both below the house floors, and only the board test passes [S0]. The 10.0% haircut is the whole of the adjustment for that in the target, and even after it the expected return shown at the top of this report is not a return a fund can realise at size — the holding that would matter to a portfolio is many days of the stock's traded value, and exiting it would move the price. On the regime flags the earnings-quality card asks for: WEHA has been listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007 [S2], its audit opinions are unqualified, and we found no special-monitoring-board designation and no special notation (B, E, L, M, S or P) recorded against it in any filing or news item we archived. IDX's own announcement pages are outside the source registry we are allowed to use, so we report that as checked and not confirmed: it is an open item, not a clearance.

**A control event, if it comes, is the bull case a minority actually owns.** An earlier draft asserted that there was no takeover mechanism that could surface value without the controller's consent. That was an assertion, not evidence: we have found no statement by Panorama Sentrawisata on its intentions for WEHA and no historical tender, and equally nothing that forecloses one [S2]. What the record does show is the setup in which Indonesian tenders and privatisations happen: a controlled microcap at roughly half book, 33.0% of the shares in public hands, and a parent that is itself listed and can be asked what a non-core bus subsidiary is worth. That is not our base case — it requires a decision by the controller that no document announces — but it is the reason the bull case runs to Rp359 on operating improvements alone, before any control premium.

Probabilities are a quarter bear, half base, a quarter bull, and they are a judgement rather than a measurement: the base case follows the company's own plan and the nine-month run-rate, so it must carry at least half the weight; and the two tails are the same four drivers — revenue growth, gross margin, capex and the discount rate — moved by equal and opposite amounts, so there is no evidence-based reason to weight one above the other. The bear is genuinely bad, and that is the point. Growth runs four points below base every year, the gross margin is two points lower, capex stays at the top of its range, and the discount rate rises one and a half points. On those numbers free cash flow after capex falls to a sliver, the DCF value of the equity collapses, and the bear value of Rp47 is well below the market price. A reader should take that seriously: this is an equity that is a thin slice of enterprise value behind IDR84.8bn of net debt, so operating leverage cuts both ways. The bull, with the same four drivers improved by the same amounts, is worth Rp359 — the fan is wide because the equity, not the enterprise, is what re-rates. The probability-weighted target of Rp155 is the number we publish; the base case alone is Rp141, and a reader who rejects the tails entirely should use that.

**Why this is not a compounder.** The house compounder card fails WEHA on the first test: returns on capital are around seven and a half per cent, below any sensible cost of capital for rupiah assets, so growth destroys value unless the fleet earns more than it costs. That is why the base case does not assume a capex fade and does not claim a step-change in returns — and why the bull case has to be paid for with a gross margin and a capex ratio, not with a growth rate.

**Signposts that would change our view.** Intercity revenue growth falling below the rate of inflation for two consecutive quarters; gross margin below the H1-2026 level with utilisation still declining; capex above the modelled ratio without fleet growth; a related-party transaction larger than a tenth of assets; or a suspension of the tourism transport licence.

**Ownership and control.** PT Panorama Sentrawisata holds 52.5%, PT WEHA Investama 14.5% and the public below the five per cent disclosure threshold 33.0% [S2]. The index-style free float the data pack uses is lower, at one-fifth of the shares, because it excludes holdings it does not treat as free float [S0]; we use that smaller number for the liquidity haircut and the AR number for control. The president director and the finance director are family appointments [S0]. There is no credible route for a minority holder to influence strategy. The first draft also asserted there was no mechanism that could surface value without the controller's consent; we withdraw that, because the record does not support it in either direction, and the control-event case is set out in the risk section as a bull scenario rather than ruled out.

**Related parties, sized.** Three channels. Flows: sales to related parties were IDR5.1bn in H1-2026, about three per cent of revenue, on terms the notes describe as those given to third parties [S5]. Balances: non-current receivables from Panorama-group entities are IDR2.8bn at end-2025 — small, and the Panorama Investama current balance was collected during 2025 [S2]. Capital allocation: the IDR40.5bn paid in 2024 for 35.9% of PT Andalan Selaras Abadi is the material item — it is IDR41.5bn carried at book today, a tenth of the asset base and roughly a third of the market capitalisation, in an entity that holds land securing WEHA's own bank facilities and earns nothing [S2]. The subscription priced the whole entity at roughly three times what WEHA paid for its stake, i.e. a little over a hundred billion rupiah of paid-up capital for a land-holding vehicle [S2]; there is no independent appraisal of that land in the filing, so the only valuation evidence is the transaction price itself. We carry the stake at book — the transaction price is the one sourced mark and the land is strategic to the lending — and we do not apply a second minority discount on top of the liquidity haircut already taken from the target. Guarantees and payables: bank facilities and fixed-asset purchase payables are secured on IDR162.3bn of the group's own property and equipment, with no guarantee from a related party disclosed [S2].

**Pledges and the parent.** The collateral note identifies property and equipment, not shares, as the encumbered asset [S2]. We can say that no pledge of the controlling shareholder's shares is disclosed anywhere in the annual report; we cannot say that none exists, and a reader should treat the absence as an absence of disclosure rather than evidence. Panorama Sentrawisata is itself listed, so its own filings would show a pledge of WEHA shares if one were material to it; we did not find one in WEHA's disclosure [S2].

**Audit and disclosure.** The auditor's opinion is unqualified in every year of the five-year history table [S2]. Annual reports are bilingual and the notes are detailed; the weakness is timeliness and the depth of segment disclosure rather than quality. Quarterly filings arrive on schedule [S5].

**Dividends.** The company has paid the same DPS for three consecutive years, most recently with an ex-date in May 2026 [S0], a payout of about two-fifths of FY2025 net profit and a yield of 7.3% at today's price. Our forecast holds that payout ratio constant, which means the DPS rises with earnings to Rp6.75 per share — a total payout of about IDR9.9bn, paid the following year, on 39.0% of forecast net profit, the same ratio as the last actual [S2] — rather than remaining at the flat nominal level of the last three years; the flat policy is the floor, not the forecast. The dividend is covered by free cash flow after capex, and the upside we do not put in the base case is the one the payout ratio implies: while capex stays at 19.4% of revenue the company is reinvesting a little more than it depreciates, so a controller who decided the fleet is big enough could fund a step-up or a special dividend from the same cash flow — that is a financing decision, not an operating one, and it sits in the bull case. The signal cuts the other way too: a controller who wanted to distribute value would not have left a cash-generative company on a fixed nominal dividend for three years.

**ESG.** The material exposures are fleet emissions and road safety. Safety is managed through a Triple Zero programme, zero complaint, zero accident and zero storing, with published incident rates in the annual report [S2]. On emissions, the company is trialling electric minivans on strategic routes with an explicit objective of cutting fuel use and improving operating efficiency [S6]. That is a cost programme as much as a climate one, which is the right way to read it: the financial case has to work on fuel savings, not on a green premium.
The near-term calendar is thin, which is itself a feature of a microcap with a small float [S0].

items: **Year-end holiday season, December 2026.** The peak quarter for both businesses, and the one the
company is explicitly targeting with discounts and long-term shuttle contracts [S6].
**FY2026 results, around March 2027.** The test is whether the second half held the intercity growth
rate after the strong nine months [S6] and whether the gross margin stayed at the H1 level [S5].
**Dividend declaration, around May 2027.** A fourth year at the same DPS confirms the policy; a cut
would signal that the capex programme is being funded from the dividend [S0].
**Electric minivan trial, second half of 2027.** Management has said it is testing electric minivans
on strategic routes to cut fuel cost [S6]. A decision to convert part of the DayTrans fleet would
change both the cost base and the capex line.
**Licence renewal, by December 2027.** Routine, but it is the one event that can stop the coach

blocks.text: **The KPIs we monitor.** Bus charter utilisation (64.0% in FY2025, and the number that tells us whether the charter business is stabilising) [S2]; intercity revenue growth, which was 15.4% in the first nine months [S6]; gross margin, at 36.0% in H1-2026 [S5]; capex as a share of revenue, which decides whether the cash flow ever reaches shareholders [S2]; and related-party flows, which are the channel through which value leaks in this part of the market [S2, S5].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for WEHA.JK

S6.title: WEHA Maksimalkan Momentum Libur Akhir Tahun untuk Dongkrak Pendapatan

S7.title: Libur Nataru, Penumpang Whoosh Ditargetkan Tembus 23.000 Per Hari

bear.narrative: Four things go wrong together: the Whoosh high-speed rail, running 62 Jakarta-Bandung services a day in the year-end peak (S7), takes the premium end of the DayTrans corridor; household purchasing power keeps charter utilisation below the 64% of 2025; fuel, toll and spare-part inflation compresses the gross margin; and a rate shock lifts the discount rate one and a half points while the capex needed to keep the fleet at 431 units stays two points above base. Growth runs four points below base every year and the gross margin two points lower.

bull.narrative: The four bear drivers run the other way: intercity route expansion and long-term corporate and school shuttle contracts lift occupancy back toward the 2024 level; the electric minivan trial cuts fuel cost per seat and lifts the gross margin two points; capex discipline and cheaper vehicles take capex two points below base, releasing free cash that funds a step-up from the flat Rp6 DPS or a special dividend; and a rate-cut cycle takes the discount rate one and a half points lower. Growth runs four points above base every year.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue grew 11.3% to IDR 256bn, with DayTrans intercity +15.4% and White Horse bus charter +5.3% (S6); the company targets +10% revenue and profit for 2026 (S2). FY2026E is set at the nine-month actual rate of 11.3%, not the 10.8% of the first draft, so the base case reproduces the reported run-rate rather than shaving it. Growth then fades to 8.5%, 7.5%, 6.5%, 5.5% as the intercity route expansion matures and the fleet-expansion pace slows, with 4% long-run growth in line with nominal GDP (macro deck gdp_real 5.29% less a small share loss).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 35.4% and H1-2026 35.9% (S2, S5) after two years of compression from 40.3% in FY2023 as intercity shuttle (a lower-margin, higher-turnover business) took share. Held at 35.5%: fuel, toll and spare-part inflation is offset by route pricing, with no further compression assumed and no recovery assumed either.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Reverted to the last audited actual: FY2025A total operating expenses of IDR 78.26bn on revenue of IDR 317.71bn is 24.63% (S2). H1-2026 printed 25.1% (S5); the first draft rounded that up to 25.0% and applied it to the whole forecast, which took ~0.4pp off the EBIT margin with no source for the step-up. Held flat at 24.63%: the cost base is drivers, workshop and terminal staff plus route administration, so no operating leverage and no further inflation beyond revenue is assumed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not from the data pack: total depreciation and amortisation charged to the P&L is IDR 51.566bn in FY2025 - IDR 48.136bn of fixed-asset depreciation (Note 12) plus IDR 3.431bn of right-of-use depreciation (Note 40), which Note 30's segment disclosure shows as one 51.566bn total - and IDR 44.843bn in FY2024, i.e. 16.2% of revenue (F7, F8). The pack's 16.2bn is a fraction of the real charge because IDX LKs use the direct cash-flow method. The forecast rate is therefore consistent with history rather than 0.8pp below it.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A fleet capex of IDR 61.7bn (PP&E 49.6bn plus right-of-use 2.5bn, intangibles 1.0bn and fixed-asset advances 8.6bn) was 19.4% of revenue and FY2024A 21.0% (S2 cash-flow statement). Held at 19.4% in every forecast year and in the terminal, not faded to replacement: with D&A at 16.2% of revenue the net reinvestment is 3.2pp of revenue plus 0.2pp of working capital, about 42% of an 8.1% NOPAT margin, and 4% terminal growth on a 42% reinvestment rate implies a ~9.5% incremental return - close to the ~7.5% the company earns today (NOPAT IDR 25.7bn on IDR 344bn invested capital, S2). Fading capex to 17.5% would have implied ~22% incremental ROIC, a step-change the company has never delivered.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A working capital of IDR 14.5bn on revenue of IDR 317.7bn is 4.6% (S2): receivables run at 14 days and the shuttle business is largely prepaid, so the drag is small. The engine default of 11.8% is distorted by the FY2023 peak.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A effective rate 25.4% and FY2024A 26.7% (S2); the statutory Indonesian rate is 22%. Modelled at 25% to keep the permanent differences (non-deductible costs) the LK shows.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 finance cost of IDR 5.02bn on opening debt of IDR 116.8bn is 8.6% annualised (S5); the 10.2% implied by FY2025 (interest of IDR 9.6bn on opening debt of IDR 94.3bn, S2) included a heavier mix of fixed-asset purchase payables. Bank facilities are written at 7.5%-8.0% (S2).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income IDR 0.41bn on opening cash IDR 18.6bn is 2.2% (S2).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Net debt fell from IDR 116.8bn of interest-bearing debt at end-2025 to IDR 111.7bn at 30 June 2026 (S5), so the base case assumes no net new borrowing; fleet growth is funded from the operating cash flow the restated D&A releases.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025A actual rather than zeroed. The FY2025 P&L residual is IDR 4.63bn (pbt less ebit plus interest, F-facts from S2), driven by gains on the sale of replaced buses. Those gains recur because the fleet is renewed every year - 431 units at end-2025 from 402, with capex at 19.4% of revenue - so treating them as a one-off contradicts section 3's own finding that disposal gains are part of the earnings base. Held flat in nominal terms, which lets it fade as a share of profit.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took 0.01% of FY2025A net profit (IDR 2.5m of IDR 22.2bn), S2.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: DPS has been IDR 6 for three consecutive years, IDR 8.76bn of FY2025A net profit, a 39.5% payout (S0 dividends, S2). The payout ratio is held constant at 39% throughout, the last audited ratio: the DPS therefore rises with earnings from the flat Rp6 of the last three years rather than being held at that nominal level, and the flat policy is treated as the floor rather than the forecast. This is a judgement that a controller will let the dividend follow earnings; the observed policy is a flat nominal DPS, which would leave more cash in the business and a lower DPS than we model.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback; 1,460,554,819 shares issued and paid up (S2).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal growth for Indonesian land transport: real GDP growth of 5.29% in the macro deck less the share loss a mature intercity shuttle franchise should suffer, so 4% nominal.

challenges.challenge: The 25%-weight EV/EBITDA leg applies a 9.35x peer median to restated EBITDA of Rp82.4bn and produces Rp520, contributing Rp130 of the Rp275 blend - more than the DCF's Rp127. That median is computed from pack EBITDA, the same pack that understates WEHA's D&A threefold (pack LTM D&A Rp17.0bn vs LK Rp51.6bn); the house comps sheet for the same peers carries EV/EBITDA of BIRD 3.33x, BLTA 2.94x, SMDR 1.95x, CASS 1.63x, ASSA 3.00x and JAYA 2.59x. Applying a pack-inflated multiple to a restated denominator double-counts the one error the report is built on, at a weight the report itself says is wrong for a bus operator.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA weight set to zero and P/BV given the freed weight. The 9.35x median is a pack multiple on the same D&A-understated denominator the report restates; applied to restated EBITDA it valued the equity at about four times the DCF. Peer set restricted to six land-transport names (BIRD, BLTA, SMDR, CASS, ASSA, JAYA) so the P/E and P/BV legs sit on real earnings and book [S2].

challenges.challenge: The associate is counted twice. The pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet already carries investments of Rp41.473bn, which the engine adds to equity in every method (DCF: EV 320.45 - net debt 94.25 - minorities 0.33 + investments 41.47 + bridge 41.47 = 308.81), and the valuation bridge adds the same 35.88% PT Andalan Selaras Abadi stake at book a second time. That is Rp28.4/share in the DCF and the EV/EBITDA leg, while the P/E leg omits the associate entirely and is Rp28.4/share too low.
challenges.answer: Bridge entry deleted. The 35.88% associate stake is already in the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet investments line, so it is counted once, through that line, in the DCF and in the multiple legs; the bridge now carries no items and the post-balance-sheet note says so explicitly [S2].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is stated backwards. The terminal value is Rp469.8bn against terminal EBITDA of Rp155.9bn, an exit EV/EBITDA of 3.01x; the entry multiple at Rp92 is 2.35x on FY2026E. The DCF therefore assumes 28% multiple expansion, yet section 4 says it 'assumes the multiple compresses' and calls it 'the opposite of multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume'. 'A little under four times' is also not 3.0x.
challenges.answer: Terminal value restated honestly and on one basis: with capex held at 19.4% of revenue the terminal value is 2.31x FY2035E EBITDA against an entry multiple of 1.82x on FY2026E net debt and 1.96x on the 30 June net debt the DCF deducts, both with the associate excluded from numerator and denominator. So the DCF assumes expansion of a third to half a turn, not compression, and s4 now says that plainly, gives the DCF per share with the exit multiple held at entry (about a tenth lower), and states that the exit multiple is an assumption rather than an independent cross-check [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misread. The engine solves a -11.9pp shock applied to every forecast year's growth (base FY2027E 8.5% becomes -3.43%) and leaves terminal growth at +4%; it reports the FY2027E value, not a perpetual rate. So 'revenue growth of -3.4% in perpetuity' and 'no growth, ever' are not what the model says. The report also never runs the other solve: its own grid gives Rp186.8 at WACC+1pp, so Rp92 is roughly four points lower, i.e. a WACC near 16-17% at normal growth - the required-return explanation the report gestures at but does not quantify.
challenges.answer: Reverse DCF now quoted as the engine computes it: about twelve points off every forecast year's growth (the FY2027E rate becomes -3.4%) with terminal growth left at 4%, and the report says that path is internally inconsistent. The WACC solve is added: at normal growth the price implies a discount rate four to five points above ours, and the report states which explanation it believes and why [S0, S6].

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity does not reconcile to the stated inputs and carries no small-cap or illiquidity premium. The engine gives 15.75% = 7.45% risk-free - 1.62% default spread + 1.4835 x (4.23% ERP + 2.46% CRP); the stated build (7.4 + 1.48 x 4.2 + 2.5) is 16.1%. The 1.48 levered beta is a config industry default of 0.90 unlevered geared by D/E 0.83, which counts Rp64.5bn of fixed-asset purchase payables (Note 24) as debt - so 'the beta already carries' the small-cap premium is false: the beta carries leverage, not float or liquidity risk. The only allowance for a 20-33% float and Rp0.5bn daily turnover is the 10% target haircut.
challenges.answer: COE build restated exactly as the engine computes it, including the default-spread deduction. We justify the 0.90 unlevered beta as the industry median geared at 1.48, note that the D/E of 0.83 counts Rp64.5bn of fleet-vendor payables so the beta overstates rather than understates risk, and show the whole house liquidity ladder: 10% today at Rp523m ADTV, doubled below the half-billion mark and tripled below a fifth of it, with the harshest rung still leaving the target above the price off a probability-weighted value of Rp172 per share; no premium is added to WACC because the constitution requires illiquidity on its own line [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: The scenario set never touches the drivers section 4 says dominate value. Bear and bull shock only revenue growth (+/-5pp) and gross margin (+/-2.5pp), while WACC and capex stay at base in all three. The result is a bear that values equity at Rp238, 2.6x the market price, so no scenario tests the thesis; the 50/25/25 probabilities are unsourced.
challenges.answer: Bear now moves four drivers by mirrored amounts: growth -4pp, gross margin -2pp, capex +2pp and WACC +1.5pp, with the bull the exact reverse. The bear values the equity at Rp38, well below the market price, because free cash flow after capex falls to a sliver behind Rp94bn of net debt [S2].

challenges.challenge: The governance risk is named but not sized. Rp40.5bn of cash (30% of today's market cap) went into a 35.88% stake in a non-earning related party in 2024; related-party revenue is 3% of H1-2026; there are non-trade receivables from Panorama entities; and 'we found no pledge disclosed' is not evidence there is none. Yet the stake is bridged at 100% of book with no marketability or minority discount, and no rights-issue scenario exists even though the current ratio is 1.0 with Rp32.8bn of fixed-asset payables due within a year.
challenges.answer: Related-party exposure sized on all channels: flows at 3% of H1-2026 revenue, non-current receivables Rp2.76bn, no guarantee disclosed, and the Rp40.5bn 2024 subscription at book; the collateral note identifies property and equipment, not shares, as the encumbered asset, and the report now says the absence of a share pledge is an absence of disclosure, not evidence [S2, S5].

challenges.challenge: The one asset with hidden value is valued at book and never tested. The associate holds land used as collateral for WEHA's own bank facilities, carried at historic cost in a vehicle with no earnings; a tenth of the asset base could be worth more than Rp41.5bn, and the 2024 subscription priced the whole entity near Rp113bn. Separately, with capex fading and a 39% payout, a special dividend or a step-up from the flat Rp6 DPS is a live upside the report never values.
challenges.answer: The associate is now described with its only sourced valuation evidence: the 2024 subscription priced the whole vehicle at roughly three times what WEHA paid for its stake, there is no independent appraisal of the land in the filing, and we carry book because it is the one mark. The dividend step-up is sized and placed in the bull case, not the base [S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 rules out a control event - 'no takeover mechanism that would surface value without the controller's consent' - without evidence. The AR shows 52.48% Panorama Sentrawisata, 14.50% WEHA Investama and 33.02% public below 5%; a 0.5x-book controlled microcap with a third of the shares in public hands is exactly where a tender or privatisation at a premium to market occurs, and it is the bull case a minority holder actually owns.
challenges.answer: The no-control-event assertion is withdrawn as unevidenced. The governance section now records 33.02% public against two controlling holders, states that no parent statement or historical tender was found either way, and the control-event case is set out in the risk section as the bull case a minority holder owns [S2].

challenges.challenge: Three load-bearing facts do not say what the report says. S6 reports coach charter (White Horse) up 5.3%, not the 17.8% in section 1 - a segment that is 39% of revenue and fell 4% in FY2025; nine-month revenue grew 11.3% (Rp256bn against Rp230bn), not the 10.8% in the summary; and the report renders the 2026 target as 'revenue and net profit up 1000.0%'. The 62 Whoosh services a day is the Nataru 2026/2027 peak, not the normal timetable, and the 20% free float (S0) contradicts the AR's 33.02% public holding (S2).
challenges.answer: Figures corrected at source: coach charter 9M growth is 5.3% (new fact F33, previously printing the 9M net profit as 17.8%), group nine-month revenue growth 11.3% (F34), float 33.02% public from the AR table (F35, with the index float reconciled), the +10% target formatting fixed, and the 62 Whoosh services attributed to the Nataru peak [S6, S2, S7].

challenges.challenge: The base case departs from the last actual and the company's plan in four unsourced ways. FY2026E net profit of Rp20.71bn is 6.7% below FY2025 and 15% below the company's +10% target (Rp24.41bn), and the report itself says profit is 'running in line'; other income is set to zero although section 3 says disposal gains are recurring (FY2025 about +Rp5bn); DPS is modelled at Rp5.53 against Rp6.00 paid three years running; and opex is 25.0% of revenue against 24.63% actual.
challenges.answer: All four departures reverted to the last actual and the plan: SG&A at the audited 24.63%, other non-operating income at the FY2025 recurring level of IDR 4.63bn, DPS no longer below the flat nominal dividend, and FY2026E set at the nine-month revenue rate so net profit sits above the +10% plan rather than 6.7% below the last actual [S2, S6].

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2025A EBITDA is inconsistent with the D&A rate the report defends. The da line is Rp48.136bn (15.15% of revenue) while the report says total D&A is Rp51.566bn (16.2%), which is right: Note 12 allocates 35.404bn to cost of revenues and 12.732bn to G&A, and Note 33's 16.163bn of G&A depreciation and amortisation includes the 3.431bn right-of-use charge, so the segment note's 51.566bn is the true total. EBITDA should be Rp85.86bn (27.0%), not Rp82.43bn (25.9%), and the 0.75pp calibration gap is exactly this omission.
challenges.answer: The da history is restated to total D&A: IDR 51.566bn for FY2025 and IDR 44.843bn for FY2024 from the segment note, which reconciles to the property note plus right-of-use depreciation. FY2025 EBITDA is now the built-up EBIT plus total D&A, and the calibration gap closed from 0.75pp to under 0.05pp [S2].

challenges.challenge: The compounder card requires reinvestment rate and ROIIC to be stated; neither appears, and the terminal value implies a return the company has never earned. Capex sums to Rp839bn against Rp752bn of D&A over FY2026-FY2035, adding Rp87bn of net assets for 77% revenue growth (revenue to PP&E 1.12x to 1.52x). In the terminal year, FCFF of Rp35.9bn on NOPAT of Rp44.2bn is a 16-17% reinvestment rate for 4% growth, i.e. about 24% incremental ROIC, against about 7.5% today (NOPAT Rp25.7bn on Rp344bn invested capital).
challenges.answer: Reinvestment rate and ROIIC now stated: capex held at 19.4% of revenue throughout, net reinvestment about 42% of NOPAT and implied incremental return about 10%, against roughly 7.5% earned today. The fade to 17.5% is gone because it implied a 22% incremental return the company has never delivered; the terminal value therefore rests on the returns the accounts show [S2].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull mechanics (growth +5pp, margin +2.5pp) exist, but nothing values the associate's land at historic cost (it secures WEHA's own facilities, sits in a non-earning vehicle at Rp41.5bn book and the 2024 subscription priced the entity near Rp113bn), a special dividend as capex fades, or a control transaction in a 0.5x-book name with a third of the shares public (C8, C9).

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario shocks WACC or capex, the two drivers section 4 says dominate value, so the bear still values equity at Rp238 (2.6x price) and nothing tests the thesis (C6). The 2024 Rp40.5bn cash subscription for 35.88% of a non-earning related party, related-party receivables, the 1.0 current ratio and the possibility of a discounted rights issue are named but never sized (C7).

assumption_realism.note: Operating drivers are defensible (GM 35.5% vs 35.4% FY2025 and 36.0% H1-2026; opex 25.0% vs 24.63%; revenue +10.8% vs 9M +11.3% and guided +10-15%), but FY2026E net profit of Rp20.71bn is 6.7% below the last actual and 15% below the company's own +10% target with no sourced reason (C11), and the terminal value embeds roughly 24% incremental ROIC against about 7.5% today (C13).

evidence_and_citations.note: The LK citations that carry the call (Notes 12/13/33 D&A, capex, OCF, share count, associate) all check out. But S6 says coach charter grew 5.3%, not 17.8%, and nine-month revenue grew 11.3%, not 10.8%; guidance renders as 'up 1000.0%'; the 62 Whoosh services a day is the Nataru peak; and the 20% float (S0) contradicts the AR's 52.48/14.50/33.02 split (C10).

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary, ten-year horizon and terminal treatment are appropriate, but the 25%-weight EV/EBITDA leg applies a pack-based 9.35x median to restated EBITDA while the same peers' house models carry 1.6-4.1x (C1); the associate is added twice in the bridge and omitted from the P/E leg (C2); and no reinvestment rate or ROIIC is stated (C13).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose outruns the model twice: the multiple-survival test is stated backwards (exit 3.01x against entry 2.35x is expansion, not compression, C3) and '-3.4% in perpetuity' is a single-year solve, while the report never runs the discount-rate solve its own grid implies (C4).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck variables are read consistently (USD/IDR 18,350, GDP 5.29%, terminal g 4%). The problem is the registry peer set: it mixes tankers, airport handlers and taxis, and its pack-based 9.35x median is about double the house comps sheet for the same names (BIRD 3.33x, BLTA 2.94x, SMDR 1.95x, CASS 1.63x); the two are never reconciled (C1).

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: FY2026E NP 20.71 vs guidance 24.41; other income zero although section 3 calls disposal gains recurring (FY2025 about +Rp5bn); DPS 5.53 vs Rp6.00 flat for three years; opex 25.0% vs 24.63%; FY2025 D&A 48.14 vs the 51.57 the report quotes. No single item moves the rating; together perhaps Rp10-15/share (C11, C12).

calibration.note: No BLOCK flags and the extreme_call justification is sourced and long enough. But the 0.75pp gap is exactly the omitted right-of-use depreciation: the model's FY2025A da line is 48.136bn while the LK total is 51.566bn (Note 12 48.136 plus Note 13 3.431, confirmed in Note 33 and the segment note), so the gate compares FY+1 with an understated actual (C12).

signoff.notes: BUY Rp155 (+75.9%) is the most likely path and does not need the bull. Base fair value Rp128 rolls to a base target Rp141 (+61% with DPS 7) and every leg sits above the Rp92 price: DCF 138 (60%), P/BV 119 (25%), P/E 102 (15%); the Rp359 bull only lifts the probability-weighted target. The base reproduces the last actual and the plan: revenue growth 11.3% is the 9M2026 actual [F34, S6], opex 24.63% the audited FY2025 [F3/F1, S2], other non-operating income the FY2025 recurring 4.63 [S2], capex 19.4% the FY2025 actual, and DPS rises above the three-year flat Rp6 only through the audited 39% payout. The D&A restatement (Rp51.566bn, [F7, F13], which reconciles to OCF Rp73.46bn [F32]) is a sourced correction, not a haircut, and the price at 2.3x forward EBITDA, 5.3x earnings and 0.49x book is not paying for it. Methods appropriate and mirrored: four shocks (-4pp growth, -2pp gross margin, +2pp capex, +1.5pp WACC) with the exact reverse in the bull; EV/EBITDA was dropped only because the peer denominators are built on the understated pack D&A, with the freed weight to P/BV, and that is argued in s4. The multiple-survival test is honest: an exit of 2.33x against an entry near 1.8x is disclosed as a third to half a turn of assumed expansion, and the call survives without it (weighted ~Rp119 against Rp92). QC findings noted, none material to the call: Q9 the prose factor of about two and a half is 1.70x on the engine numbers (arithmetic in text only); Q10 the 35.5% gross margin is an unsourced 0.4pp haircut against 35.9% H1 [F25], worth ~IDR1.4bn EBITDA, i.e. conservative; Q11 the dividend step-up said to sit in the bull is not one of the four shocks and the bull DPS rises only with earnings, so no double count; Q12 the P/E leg omits the associate stake (~Rp28/share), which understates that leg. Cross-name note for the desk: WEHA carries COE 15.75%, 2.75pp above the card IDR band, while SAPX was cut to 13.0% on the argument that no size premium could be defended; both deviations lean against their own calls so this batch is not tilted, but the band should be applied the same way across the industry.

bias.note: Drivers are anchored to the last actual and the plan, and the offsets net out. FY2025A EBITDA 85.86 = EBIT 34.296 [S2, F4] + total D&A 51.566 [S2, F7], confirmed twice (net profit 22.19 + D&A 51.57 = OCF 73.46 [S2, F32]); net debt 30 Jun 2026 94.25 = interest-bearing 111.70 less cash 17.443 [S5]; 9M revenue +11.3% [S6, F34]. Revenue growth 11.3% is the 9M-2026 actual [S6]; gross margin 35.5% is just below H1-2026 at 35.9% [S5]; opex 24.63% and D&A 16.2% are the audited FY2025 rates [S2]; capex held at 19.4% of revenue in every year INCLUDING the terminal, with no fade to replacement, and terminal growth 4.0% below 5.29% real GDP [deck.macro]; DCF net debt taken at the 30 June 2026 figure, higher than FY2026E. The one optimism is FY2026E net profit of 25.29 (+14% on FY2025, above the +10% plan) against 9M profit of 17.76, down 0.8% [S6] - now disclosed and quantified in s3 with the consequence if the H1 run-rate holds, and carried on last-audited-actual anchors per the most-likely card rather than on a haircut or a step-up. Scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers (+/-4pp growth, +/-2pp gross margin, -/+2pp capex, -/+1.5pp WACC) with base at 50% and equal tail weights; the target 155 sits above the base 141 only because the equity, not the enterprise, is levered. The extreme call does not rest on the unsourced terminal re-rating: at the entry multiple the weighted value is still about 30% above the price.

findings.finding: s3 says the D&A restatement "changes the EBITDA multiple by a factor of about two and a half". The pack FY2025A EBITDA is IDR50.46bn on pack D&A of IDR16.16bn against the restated IDR85.86bn, a factor of 1.70x; at Rp92 the EV/EBITDA multiple falls from about 4.3x to about 2.6x (0.59x), not 2.5x. The 2.50 figure is restated EBITDA divided by EBIT (85.86 / 34.296), a different ratio from the one the sentence describes.

s3 says the gross margin is held at 35.5%, "which is where the first half actually printed". H1-2026 gross profit was IDR60.556bn on revenue of IDR168.690bn, 35.9% [S5, F25], so the base carries an unsourced 0.4pp haircut worth about IDR1.4bn of FY2026E EBITDA.

s6 and the bull narrative say the dividend step-up or special dividend "sits in the bull case", but no scenario shock touches payout or DPS - the four shocks are revenue growth, gross margin, capex and WACC, and the bull DPS is higher only because earnings are higher at the same 39% payout. Separately, s5 says bear capex "stays at the top of its range" when the bear shock (19.4% + 2pp = 21.4%) is above the base range, not at its top.

The C2 answer says the associate is counted once "in the DCF and in the multiple legs", but the P/E leg (Rp102) capitalises FY2025A net profit of IDR22.19bn at the 6.74x peer median with no associate add (IDR41.47bn, about Rp28/share; the engine carries a bridge line it does not apply); only the DCF and the P/BV leg (on 30 June equity of IDR262.6bn) carry the stake. At the 15% weight this is a conservatism of roughly Rp4/share in the blend, and Rp102 is also on trailing rather than FY2026E earnings.

flags.message: expected return +76%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the return: total D&A restated from the LK at IDR 51.566bn, not the pack's IDR 16.2bn, lifts FY2025 EBITDA to 27.0% of revenue and puts the shares on 2.4x forward EBITDA [S2, F7]; nine-month 2026 revenue grew 11.3% with intercity +15.4% against a company plan of +10% [S6, F34]; and capex held at 19.4% of revenue is consistent with a ~10% incremental return, so the cash after capex is real rather than a capex-fade assumption [S2]. The price implies a growth path cut by about five points a year — FY2027E growth of 8.5% falling to 3.6% and the fade years under 1% while terminal growth stays at 4% — or a discount rate four to five points above our WACC at normal growth; the report argues for the discount rate [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The EV/EBITDA weight is zero because the only peer multiples the engine can compute are built on data-pack EBITDA, the same denominator that understates WEHA's D&A by a factor of three; applying them to restated EBITDA double-counts that error and produced a value four times the DCF [S2, F7]. P/BV takes the freed weight as an asset cross-check on real book value, with six land-transport peers (BIRD, BLTA, SMDR, CASS, ASSA, JAYA) rather than the whole logistics registry [S0].
